title: OpenClaw launches an AI performance benchmark that it argues is more realistic than others
summary: OpenClaw, working with a host of other industry players including Hugging Face, Nvidia, Red Hat, Google and Amazon, Tuesday rolled out an AI performance benchmark called ShellBench. OpenClaw’s position is that the benchmark will compare various AI models (it will soon look at a total of 24) and test them on complex queries, ones that should better replicate the kind of complicated tasks that an enterprise would perform. “Ask an AI agent to summarize a document, and it will probably do a decent job. Ask it to reconcile a handful of receipts against a spreadsheet, check which information is current, flag a suspicious payment request, and explain how it reached its answer? Maybe not so well,” said the OpenClaw post describing the new benchmark . “This kind of realistic test, one that expects an agent not just to find the right information but also to keep track of it along the way, is exactly what we’re launching ShellBench to evaluate.” Analysts and consultants said the new benchmark findings appear initially to be more useful than existing AI performance benchmarks, but it is less clear how useful those results will be. Thomas Randall , a research director at Infotech, said that he sees ShellBench as focusing on those who are building and configuring agents directly, but most enterprises instead buy their AI capabilities from various large AI vendors. “They are choosing capabilities within an enterprise platform, often with limited control over the underlying model or agent configuration. For these organizations, ShellBench offers little direct use,” Randall said. “ShellBench giving a strong score for an underlying model does not tell us the quality of output from a solution built on it. The tasks ShellBench tests are skewed toward personal knowledge work rather than heavy enterprise workflows that buyers typically evaluate for.” Are results reproducible? title: Where the software development bottleneck went
summary: It’s not often you get to talk about potato chips twice in one year in a tech column, but here we are. Back in January, I discussed a fascinating podcast that featured a guy from Frito-Lay , who had the marvelous job of speeding up the potato chip production line. In the podcast, the Frito-Lay guy, Brendan O’Donohoe, discusses Goldratt’s Theory of Constraints — the notion that all processes are limited by a small number of constraints. In my column, I noted that coding is no longer the major constraint in software development, thanks to AI, and I said that figuring out what software projects to do next would become the new hard part. Well, I was wrong about that. I was right about one thing — coding isn’t the bottleneck anymore. I had a laugh with some friends the other day. For years they used the planning poker method of estimating projects, and it worked pretty well for them. I use the past tense because they don’t use it anymore. Over the past few months, every project they tried to specify turned out to be a “1”. Coding agents can write even major product features in time spans best measured in hours, not weeks or months. Trying to figure out how long something would take had become moot, so planning poker became pointless. Stuck in code review What I was wrong about was that developers would no longer be the bottleneck. It turns out that we still are — only in a different place. Faros , a software engineering analytics platform, has shown that the bottleneck still lies in the development team’s lap , but not in the coding phase. Code is being written at such a breakneck pace that the work is stacking up in the code review stage. It used to be that teams could review code much faster than it could be written, so they monitored metrics like “Mean Time in Review (MTiR).” Teams would work to keep that time down, meaning code was reviewed quickly and efficiently. title: Seven key features of AI governance platforms
summary: Ask leaders what they prioritize in AI governance, and many will start by discussing employee policies and guidelines. Communicating AI guardrails, business objectives, and best practices to employees is important for balancing AI strategy with controls . But as pressure mounts to deliver AI business value and drive employee adoption , organizations must address additional risk areas. Leaders in IT, security, and risk management also are worried about shadow AI , data access privileges, intellectual property leaks, AI debt , and increasing costs . “The CIO should hold the keys for data access, privilege management, and security,” says Gerrit Kazmaier, president of product and technology at Workday . “The biggest challenge for any CIO is how they can secure AI, trust that any AI is behaving lawfully based on the governance workflows, and determine which agents are auditable, traceable, and secure.” What is AI governance? You don’t have to brainstorm what goes into AI governance. TDWI defines AI governance broadly as “a set of policies, processes, roles, and controls an organization puts in place to ensure its AI systems behave as intended, produce outcomes that are fair and reliable, and operate within legal and ethical boundaries.” Some AI governance best practices include inventorying use cases, assigning ownership responsibilities to AI agent owners, and integrating data governance practices . There are also standards to review. The NIST AI 100-1 standard , known as the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, has a Govern category with seven subcategories covering legal and regulatory requirements, trustworthy AI, risk-based procedures, monitoring, inventory of AI systems, and life-cycle management. Other related standards include the ISO/IEC AI Standards and Cloud Security Alliance’s AI Control Matrix . title: Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
summary: Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries. In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset. The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual. Need to buy time “For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint,” Cisco president and CPO Jeetu Patel wrote in a blog post . “You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it.” But, he asserted, this approach is “fundamentally mismatched” to AI. Security should live inside the infrastructure itself. “If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind,” he said. He noted that AI agents are getting better at discovering security vulnerabilities; for instance, startup Calif used AI to help discover the PHP2Shell flaw and a major Java bug . Dovetailing with this, the agents themselves are both a risk vector and an adversarial actor. Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he pointed out. Flaws unfold over minutes and hours, as opposed to the days and weeks of the past, but permanent fixes take time to build, test, and roll out. “We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place,” Patel said.
